chapter_theme: The city's king is praised for a reign in which only Kama's arrows are abroad, who takes his sixth share only as grace and keeps learned counsellors; the verses then turn to his two chief queens, Mikapathi and her sister Sasi, who bind his mind until the work of ruling is set aside and the world sleeps under his one umbrella.

cast.role: the king of the city, unnamed beyond நரபதி and மன்னவன்
the king's queens, a thousand in all and two above the rest
Mikapathi's younger sister, the king's other chief queen

53.reading: In the days this king guarded the world nothing but Kama's arrows mingled in the land; no fierce, fire-like killing force of spear-bearing warriors troubled his sea-bounded realm.
53.nuance: The praise of a bloodless reign names Kama's arrows as the only weapon abroad, which sets up the verses that follow, where the same arrows work inside the palace.

54.reading: The king takes his sixth share only as a duty of grace, rejoices in no harm done to the world, and brings even enemies low by making them bow, never by slaying them in anger.

claims.claim: a king's one-sixth share is his dharma, to be taken only with grace and without oppression
a king should subdue foes by making them bow, not by killing in wrath

54.nuance: The reading takes ஆறிலொன்று as the royal share of the produce and அறம் as its name; the verse says nothing of a rival measure.

55.reading: Kings find shelter in the shade at the king's feet, sages find refuge in the shade of his crown, and the world stands cool under the shade of his umbrella.

56.reading: With neither lasting foes nor a ring of hostile neighbours, the king guards himself and the earth, so there is nothing here to puzzle over.

57.reading: The king takes as kin men great in the books that unfold the truth and, like the swan that parts milk from water, keeps the world free of the common.
57.event: The king chooses learned counsellors as his kinsmen.
57.nuance: பொதுமை நீக்கினான் is the hard phrase; it may mean he put aside what is common, or what is shared, in his rule, and the sense is not fixed.

58.reading: Whatever the king does not hint at, none of the countless strangers dares to propose, and the speakers around him stay unafraid; his divisions follow in orderly array.
58.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are hard to construe; the verse seems to say that nothing is said at court except at the king's hint, and that his forces fall in as he arranges.

59.reading: His queens appear to light the royal clans, with swelling breasts whose weight bends their waists and a mastery of the arts.

60.reading: The queens are slender-waisted, broad-hipped women with reddish spots of beauty on the breast, bending like a vanci creeper with a bough of five bright flowers.

61.reading: The queens are full of desire and of shining chastity, with dark hair heavy with flowers, shoulders bright as smoke-lit flame and broad dark eyes.

62.reading: Besides the thousand wives, two stand above the rest, said to have come down from the sky and to be like lotus goddesses, beyond any words.

63.reading: The chief queen Mikapathi, sweet of speech, is joined by her younger sister Sasi, whose chaste constancy matches Indra's queen Sachi.
63.nuance: தங்கை marks Sasi as the younger sister, and the verse praises both for a chastity hard to bear; the poet's own voice carries the praise.

64.reading: The two women shine as the diadem of all flower-eared women, like the mango sprout and the asoka that bloom together in spring.

65.reading: Cherished by the king and fresh in their prattle every day, the two become single in his heart, as dear as the goddess of wealth and the goddess of learning are to a great man.
65.event: The two queens come to hold one place in the king's heart.

66.reading: The king is the life of the women and they are his; the poet asks what makes one heart run toward another, and gives the answer in the way the flower-arrowed god had ordained.
66.nuance: The verse treats the love among the three as set by Kama's design, and does not say whether the poet holds it a bond to be praised or one that binds.

67.reading: Setting aside the work of speaking justice and guarding the world, the queens bind the king's mind, like a kalpaka sprout and a creeper of desire that cannot bear their load of flowers.
67.event: The queens draw the king's mind from the work of ruling.
67.nuance: The verse says the king's ruling work is pushed outside; the narrator does not blame the queens or the king here.

68.reading: Two women, one king: he gives himself wholly in each, taking the form of Indra among goddess-like women.

69.reading: His sea-girdled earth sleeps under the shade of one white umbrella, while the king bathes in his queens' breasts, and such was the wealth of his rule.
69.nuance: The closing verse sets the single umbrella of rule beside the delight of the palace and lets them stand together as the king's 'rule-wealth' (அரசச் செல்வம்), without comment.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 244 calls the king's share one sixth of the produce and ties it to keeping dharma without lapse; 54 shows the king taking his sixth only as grace.
links.teaches: The verse puts the one-sixth rule into practice as restraint on both tax and killing, while the Tirumanthiram makes it a step on the road to release and wealth.

gains.a: The verse gains the Tirumanthiram's claim that dharma kept without lapse is the road to release as well as wealth, which its own praise of the king leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a king who actually takes only the sixth and refuses wrathful killing, so its rule has a figure who keeps it.

links.note: Kural 550 allows a king to put the cruel to death as weeding the crop; 54 has this king subdue even opponents by bowing them, and not slay in anger.
links.teaches: The couplet's weeding is the harsher rule, and the verse shows a king who treats killing as what grace avoids, so the two differ on whether death is part of a king's work.

gains.a: The verse gains a rival standard in which a king's killing counts as justified, against which his restraint reads as a choice, not a rule.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king who will not weed even his foes, showing how far a ruler can go without using death.

links.note: Kural 447 prizes counsellors who rebuke the ruler; 58 shows a court where no one proposes anything except at the king's hint.
links.teaches: The couplet praises the courtier who dares to rebuke, and the verse depicts a court where none speak unless prompted, which shows what the king gives up by having no one to correct him.

gains.a: The verse gains a measure that reveals its silent court as lacking the correction a ruler needs.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete court of obedient, fearless speakers, showing what its rebuking counsellors would stand against.

links.note: 53 says the only weapon abroad in his reign was Kama's arrows; 66 shows the same flower-arrowed god working inside the palace to join the king and the two queens.
links.teaches: The praise of a bloodless reign leads to the place where Kama's arrows land, showing the opening claim as the first note of the palace's own story.

links.note: 56 says the king guards himself and the earth; 67 has the queens draw his mind from the work of ruling.
links.teaches: The king whose guarding of the world is praised is shown giving up the work of ruling to the queens' hold on his mind, so the poem sets one claim against the other.

links.note: Kural 902 says shame follows the man whose desire for his woman makes him careless of other things; 67 has two wives bind a king so that he lets the work of ruling go.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks for any man and the verse shows the cost to a king, whose neglected work is the world's guarding, so the stakes are larger than shame.

gains.a: The verse gains a verdict on a king set aside by love, which the narrator does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler whose lapse touches a whole realm, which widens its cost beyond personal shame.

links.note: 55 puts kings and sages in the shade of the king's umbrella and feet; 69 puts the whole earth asleep under the one white umbrella while the king bathes in the queens' breasts.
links.teaches: The shade that began as the world's refuge ends as the setting for the king's pleasure, so the umbrella changes from protection to the sign of a wealth enjoyed.

links.note: Siddhar 1790 scolds the stony mind for wanting to rule the whole earth under one umbrella; 69 closes the king's praise on exactly that single umbrella and his pleasure under it.
links.teaches: The Siddhar treats the one-umbrella rule as a desire to be given up, while the poem treats it as the king's finished wealth, so the same picture means a trap in one and a reward in the other.

gains.a: The verse gains a rival reading of the one umbrella as the object of craving, against which its praise sounds partial.
gains.b: The Siddhar verse gains a king who has the whole earth under one umbrella, so its warning has a figure who is already there.

links.note: Naladiyar 3 says that kings who rode under the royal umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 69 shows a king at the height of his umbrella-wealth, with no word of what deeds will bring.
links.teaches: The quatrain says the umbrella's glory lasts only while deeds hold it up, and the verse stops at the glory without the fall, so the reader supplies the warning from the quatrain.

gains.a: The verse gains a condition on its calm, that the king's wealth lasts only while his deeds do.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king in full peace, whose praise stops where its warning would begin.

source_issues: 58 lines 2-3 and 57 line 4 (பொதுமை நீக்கினான்) are hard to construe; the readings given are tentative.
66 line 3-4 (the way the first one joined them) is obscure, and the first one is taken as Kama.
